2 Five meanings of validation
Without an outcome, “is this clustering good?” has to be split into questions that can be answered.

Internal quality. Are the clusters compact and separated according to the distance we chose?
Stability. Would a different sample of players from the same population give the same clusters?
External agreement. Do the clusters relate to information that was not used, such as listed positions or salaries?
Sensitivity. Do the clusters survive reasonable changes in the features, transformations, and distance?
Usefulness. Do the clusters answer the question that motivated them?

The first four can be computed. The fifth is a judgment, and it is the one that matters most.

3 Internal validity indexes
Let kk be the number of clusters, nn the number of observations, WW the within-cluster sum of squares, and BB the between-cluster sum of squares.
Silhouette (Tutorial 6.2): the average of si=(bi−ai)/max⁡(ai,bi)s_i=(b_i-a_i)/\max(a_i,b_i).
Calinski-Harabasz: a ratio of between to within dispersion adjusted for degrees of freedom,
CH=B/(k−1)W/(n−k).
\mathrm{CH}=\frac{B/(k-1)}{W/(n-k)}.

Larger is better. It is an F statistic in form, and it rewards the same geometry that k-means optimizes.
Davies-Bouldin: for each cluster, the worst ratio of combined spread to center separation,
DB=1k∑i=1kmaxj≠isi+sjd(𝒄i,𝒄j),
\mathrm{DB}=\frac1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}\max_{j\ne i}\frac{s_i+s_j}{d(\mathbf c_i,\mathbf c_j)},

where sis_i is the average distance of members to center 𝒄i\mathbf c_i. Smaller is better.
Dunn: the smallest distance between clusters divided by the largest cluster diameter,
Dunn=mini≠jmina∈Ci,b∈Cjd(a,b)maxldiam⁡(Cl).
\mathrm{Dunn}=\frac{\min_{i\ne j}\min_{a\in C_i,b\in C_j}d(a,b)}{\max_l\operatorname{diam}(C_l)}.

Larger is better. It uses extremes, so a single outlier can dominate it.

index_table <- function(labels, name) {
  data.frame(
    method = name,
    k = length(unique(labels)),
    silhouette = mean(silhouette(labels, D)[, "sil_width"]),
    calinski_harabasz = calinski_harabasz(X, labels),
    davies_bouldin = davies_bouldin(X, labels),
    dunn = dunn_index(D, labels)
  )
}

ward <- hclust(D, method = "ward.D2")
gmm <- Mclust(X, G = 6, modelNames = "VEI", verbose = FALSE)

results <- bind_rows(
  lapply(3:8, function(k) index_table(kmeans(X, k, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster, "k-means")),
  lapply(3:8, function(k) index_table(cutree(ward, k = k), "Ward")),
  index_table(gmm$classification, "Gaussian mixture (VEI)")

Three cautions apply to every internal index.

They reward a geometry. All four prefer compact, well-separated, roughly spherical clusters, so they favor k-means-like solutions and penalize density-based or spectral solutions that are correct for a different reason.
They depend on the distance. An index computed under Euclidean distance says nothing about a clustering built under Manhattan or Gower distance. Compare methods only on the same dissimilarity.
They do not test for the existence of clusters. Every index returns a number for a partition of uniform noise. A high value means the partition is good relative to other partitions of the same data, not that the data contain groups.

4 Stability
A clustering that changes when a few players are removed may describe fragile sample boundaries. The helper below draws bootstrap row indices, removes repeated indices, and reclusters the distinct sampled players. This is a resampling perturbation using roughly 63% of the original players, rather than an ordinary bootstrap that retains multiplicities. It holds the original scaling fixed. For each reference cluster, it records the best Jaccard match
J(A,B)=|A∩B||A∪B|
J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}

among new clusters, evaluated only on players retained in that replicate. Values near 1 indicate reproducibility under this perturbation. Values such as 0.75 are descriptive heuristics, not hypothesis-test thresholds. For a full pipeline assessment, refit preprocessing in each replicate. Section 6.7 demonstrates a complementary approach that assigns all players to each refitted solution.

kmeans_6 <- kmeans(X, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
ward_6 <- cutree(ward, k = 6)

stability_kmeans <- bootstrap_stability(
  X, function(Z) kmeans(Z, 6, nstart = 20, iter.max = 100)$cluster, reference = kmeans_6, B = 50
)
stability_ward <- bootstrap_stability(
  X, function(Z) cutree(hclust(dist(Z), method = "ward.D2"), k = 6), reference = ward_6, B = 50
)

data.frame(
  cluster = seq_len(6),
  kmeans_size = as.numeric(table(kmeans_6)),
  kmeans_jaccard = colMeans(stability_kmeans),
  ward_size = as.numeric(table(ward_6)),

5 External agreement
Two partitions can be compared with the adjusted Rand index. Count the pairs of observations that are together in both partitions, apart in both, or split; the Rand index is the share of agreeing pairs, and the adjustment subtracts what chance would produce:
ARI=∑ij(nij2)−[∑i(ai2)∑j(bj2)]/(n2)12[∑i(ai2)+∑j(bj2)]−[∑i(ai2)∑j(bj2)]/(n2),
\mathrm{ARI}=\frac{\sum_{ij}\binom{n_{ij}}{2}-\left[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\right]/\binom n2}{\frac12\left[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}+\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\right]-\left[\sum_i\binom{a_i}{2}\sum_j\binom{b_j}{2}\right]/\binom n2},

where nijn_{ij} is the number of observations in cluster ii of the first partition and cluster jj of the second, and aia_i, bjb_j are the row and column totals. It equals 1 for identical partitions and is near 0 for unrelated ones.

ARI=S−E12(TP+TQ)−E=4−2.86.5−2.8=1.23.7≈0.324.

ARI = 1: identical groupings, even if the group names or numbers differ.
ARI near 0: agreement close to the chance baseline; its expected value under that randomization is zero.
ARI below 0: less agreement than the chance baseline.

ARI is unchanged by swapping group labels because it compares who belongs together. It can also compare methods with different numbers of groups.

\mathrm{NMI}=\frac{I(A;B)}{\sqrt{H(A)\,H(B)}},

6 Sensitivity to decisions
Tutorial 6.1 listed the decisions that define a dissimilarity. The cheapest validation is to change one at a time and measure how much the partition moves.

set.seed(431)
baseline <- kmeans_6

variants <- list(
  "square-root transform of skewed rates" = {
    Z <- profiles %>% select(all_of(profile_features)) %>%
      mutate(across(c(blk_36, stl_36, oreb_36, fg3a_36, fta_36), sqrt)) %>%
      as.matrix() %>% scale()
    kmeans(Z, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
  },
  "drop scoring-volume features" = {
    Z <- X[, setdiff(profile_features, c("pts_36", "fga_36", "fta_36"))]
    kmeans(Z, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
  },
  "first five principal components" = {
    Z <- prcomp(X)$x[, 1:5]
    kmeans(Z, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
  },
  "double weight on shot selection" = {
    Z <- X
    Z[, c("three_rate", "ft_rate", "fg3a_36")] <- Z[, c("three_rate", "ft_rate", "fg3a_36")] * sqrt(2)
    kmeans(Z, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
  },
  "Manhattan distance with k-medoids" = pam(dist(X, method = "manhattan"), 6)$clustering,
  "different random seed only" = {
    set.seed(2024)
    kmeans(X, 6, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster
  }
)

data.frame(
  variant = names(variants),
  adjusted_rand_index_with_baseline = sapply(variants, function(v) adjusted_rand_index(baseline, v))
) %>%

title: 6.6 Validating, Stabilizing, and Communicating Clusters
text:
7 Communicating a clustering

7.1 What to show

Cluster profiles as a heat map of standardized centers (Tutorial 6.2) or as small bar charts, one per cluster. Radar charts are popular and hard to read; their enclosed area depends on the arbitrary order of the axes.
Example players for each cluster, chosen by playing time or by closeness to the center, and the players that fit worst.
Sizes, because a cluster of eight players is a different object from a cluster of eighty.
Uncertainty: silhouettes, mixture responsibilities, or resampling stability, so that a reader knows which boundaries are real.
A low-dimensional picture with an explicit statement of how much variance it shows.


centers <- sapply(sort(unique(kmeans_6)), function(j) colMeans(X[kmeans_6 == j, , drop = FALSE]))
colnames(centers) <- paste("Cluster", sort(unique(kmeans_6)))
two <- order(centers["blk_36", ], decreasing = TRUE)[c(1, 6)]

as.data.frame(centers[, two]) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("feature") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-feature, names_to = "cluster", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(feature = factor(feature_labels[feature], levels = feature_labels[profile_features])) %>%
  ggplot(aes(z, feature, fill = z > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#d73027", "FALSE" = "#4575b4")) +
  labs(x = "Standard deviations from the league average", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()




One communication format: standardized profiles of two clusters with their example players.






7.2 What to say
A clustering report should state, in this order:

the question, and whether the goal was archetypes or comparables;
the observations, the features, and the transformations, standardization, and weights;
the dissimilarity and the algorithm, with its settings;
how the number of clusters was chosen, and what the alternatives looked like;
the clusters, with profiles, sizes, and examples;
stability and sensitivity results, cluster by cluster; and
what the clusters do not mean.



7.3 What the clusters do not mean

Clusters describe the season’s data, not ability or value. A player in the “low-usage” cluster may have been asked to play that way.
Clusters are not causal. Two players in one cluster share a profile, not a reason for it.
Clusters are not positions, and disagreement with positions is not an error.
The number of clusters is a resolution, not a discovery.
“The algorithm found” is the wrong subject. The analyst chose the features, the distance, the method, and kk; the algorithm computed a consequence of those choices.

title: 6.6 Validating, Stabilizing, and Communicating Clusters
text:
8 Practice

Two partitions of 100 players agree on 95% of pairs. Why can their adjusted Rand index still be low?
A cluster has mean bootstrap Jaccard 0.45. What should the report say about it?
Why is a high Calinski-Harabasz value for a DBSCAN solution not evidence against DBSCAN?
Give one preprocessing change that you would expect to move the partition a great deal and one that you would expect to move it little.







TipShow answers






Most pairs are apart in any partition with several clusters, so high raw agreement is expected by chance; the adjustment removes that baseline, and the remaining agreement can be small.
That the cluster dissolves under resampling and should not be interpreted as an archetype, even if it is convenient to name.
The index rewards compact spherical clusters, which DBSCAN does not seek; a density cluster with an irregular shape scores poorly by construction.
Dropping or reweighting a block of correlated features moves the partition a great deal; changing the random seed with many restarts should move it little.

title: 6.6 Validating, Stabilizing, and Communicating Clusters
text:
9 Key takeaways

Validation without truth means internal quality, stability, external agreement, sensitivity, and usefulness; check all of them.
Internal indexes rank partitions under one distance and one geometry; they cannot certify that clusters exist.
Bootstrap Jaccard stability, reported cluster by cluster, is the most direct test of whether an archetype is real.
Adjusted Rand index and normalized mutual information compare partitions; external labels inform interpretation but are not scores.
Report the decisions, the uncertainty, and the limitations; the algorithm is not the author of the result.

title: 6.4 Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
text:
2 Clustering as a probability model
k-means says nothing about how the data were generated. A mixture model does: each observation comes from one of KK components, chosen with probabilities π1,…,πK\pi_1,\dots,\pi_K, and each component is a distribution. With Gaussian components, the density of an observation is
p(𝒙)=∑k=1Kπkϕ(𝒙∣𝝁k,Σk),∑kπk=1,p(\mathbf x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\phi(\mathbf x\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k),
\qquad
\sum_k\pi_k=1,
where ϕ\phi is the multivariate normal density. The parameters are the mixing weights, the component means, and the component covariances.

The log-likelihood of nn independent observations is
ℓ(θ)=∑i=1nlog⁡∑k=1Kπkϕ(𝒙i∣𝝁k,Σk).\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\phi(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k).
The log of a sum has no closed-form maximizer, which is why a dedicated algorithm is needed.

2.1 Responsibilities
Introduce the unobserved component label zi∈{1,…,K}z_i\in\{1,\dots,K\}. By Bayes’ rule, the posterior probability that observation ii came from component kk is the responsibility
rik=P(zi=k∣𝒙i)=πkϕ(𝒙i∣𝝁k,Σk)∑lπlϕ(𝒙i∣𝝁l,Σl).r_{ik}=P(z_i=k\mid\mathbf x_i)=\frac{\pi_k\,\phi(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{l}\pi_l\,\phi(\mathbf x_i\mid\boldsymbol\mu_l,\Sigma_l)}.
Responsibilities are the soft cluster memberships. A player with ri1=0.55r_{i1}=0.55 and ri2=0.45r_{i2}=0.45 is between two archetypes, and the model says so instead of forcing a choice.

title: 6.4 Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
text:
3 The EM algorithm
The expectation-maximization algorithm alternates two steps from an initial parameter guess.
E-step. Compute the responsibilities rikr_{ik} from the current parameters.
M-step. Maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood, which gives closed-form updates:
nk=∑irik,πk=nkn,𝝁k=1nk∑irik𝒙i,Σk=1nk∑irik(𝒙i−𝝁k)(𝒙i−𝝁k)𝖳.n_k=\sum_i r_{ik},
\qquad
\pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\mathbf x_i,
\qquad
\Sigma_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_i r_{ik}(\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)(\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k)^{\mathsf T}.
Each update is a weighted mean or weighted covariance, with the responsibilities as weights.

3.1 Why it works
For any distribution qq over the labels, Jensen’s inequality gives a lower bound on the log-likelihood,
log⁡∑kπkϕk(𝒙i)=log⁡∑kqik(πkϕk(𝒙i)qik)≥∑kqiklog⁡(πkϕk(𝒙i)qik)\begin{align}
\log \sum_k \pi_k \phi_k(\mathbf{x}_i) &= \log \sum_k q_{ik} \left( \frac{\pi_k \phi_k(\mathbf{x}_i)}{q_{ik}} \right) \\
&\ge \sum_k q_{ik} \log \left( \frac{\pi_k \phi_k(\mathbf{x}_i)}{q_{ik}} \right)
\end{align}
with equality when qik=rikq_{ik}=r_{ik}. The E-step makes the bound tight at the current parameters; the M-step raises the bound. Together they raise the log-likelihood, so exact EM does not decrease ℓ\ell. Under regularity conditions it approaches a stationary point, which need not be a global maximum. Degenerate covariance matrices are a separate failure mode. As with k-means, the local maximum reached depends on the start.






NoteWorked example: EM step by step, and why its updates work






3.2 The problem: memberships and parameters depend on each other
Suppose four players have the following values of one illustrative performance measure:
x=(1,2,5,6).x=(1,\;2,\;5,\;6).
We fit a mixture of two Gaussian components. Each component has a mean, a variance, and a mixing weight describing its share of the population.
The challenge is circular: estimating each component’s parameters requires knowing which players belong to it, but estimating membership requires knowing the parameters. EM handles this by alternating between soft membership estimates and parameter updates.

5 k-means as a limiting case
Fix every covariance to σ2I\sigma^2 I with the same σ\sigma and equal weights πk=1/K\pi_k=1/K. The responsibilities become
rik∝exp⁡(−‖𝒙i−𝝁k‖22σ2),r_{ik}\propto\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
and as σ→0\sigma\to0 each rikr_{ik} goes to 1 for the nearest center and 0 elsewhere. The E-step becomes the k-means assignment step and the M-step becomes the k-means update. Lloyd k-means corresponds to the hard-assignment limit with equal mixing weights and a common spherical variance. Finite-variance EM uses soft responsibilities, so the algorithms are not identical. Everything k-means assumes, spherical clusters of equal spread with hard membership, is a restriction the mixture model can relax.

A full covariance in pp dimensions has p(p+1)/2p(p+1)/2 parameters per component, which is 105105 for the 14-feature profiles. With 360 players and several components that is too many. mclust parameterizes each covariance through its eigendecomposition,

title: 6.4 Gaussian Mixture Models and the EM Algorithm
text:
7 The Bayesian view
The mixture model is a hierarchical model, and Lectures 4 and 5 supply the language. Write it as
zi∼Categorical(𝝅),𝒙i∣zi=k∼N(𝝁k,Σk),z_i\sim\text{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),
\qquad
\mathbf x_i\mid z_i=k\sim N(\boldsymbol\mu_k,\Sigma_k),
with priors on the parameters:
𝝅∼Dirichlet(α1,…,αK),𝝁k∼N(𝒎0,S0),Σk∼Inverse-Wishart(ν0,Ψ0).\boldsymbol\pi\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_K),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu_k\sim N(\mathbf m_0,S_0),
\qquad
\Sigma_k\sim\text{Inverse-Wishart}(\nu_0,\Psi_0).
The Dirichlet is the conjugate prior for the mixing weights, exactly as the beta was for one proportion in Lecture 4. Three things follow.

EM estimates parameters. Ordinary mixture EM maximizes the observed-data likelihood. Responsibilities condition on those fitted parameters and have a plug-in latent-variable interpretation. Full Bayes integrates over parameter uncertainty as well. Gibbs updates use full conditional distributions derived from both likelihood and priors, rather than simply randomizing the M-step.
Priors regularize. A suitable proper covariance prior or an explicit eigenvalue floor can discourage or exclude component collapse. A good initialization alone cannot guarantee protection against a singular solution. The prior must control behavior near zero variance.
The number of components can be learned. With a symmetric Dirichlet prior whose concentration α/K\alpha/K shrinks as KK grows, the model in the limit K→∞K\to\infty is a Dirichlet process mixture. For a sample of size nn, it allows 1 through nn occupied components and puts a posterior distribution on that count, which replaces the BIC search with posterior inference. The price is heavier computation and a result that depends on the concentration parameter.







NoteLabel switching



The mixture likelihood is unchanged by relabeling the components, so any sampler that explores the posterior fully will visit every permutation of the labels. Posterior means of 𝝁k\boldsymbol\mu_k are then meaningless unless the labels are aligned across draws. It is the mixture-model version of the identification problem in Lecture 5, and the usual remedies are an ordering constraint or post-hoc relabeling.

9 Key takeaways

A Gaussian mixture is a generative model whose responsibilities are soft memberships.
EM alternates computing responsibilities with weighted parameter updates and never decreases the log-likelihood.
Lloyd k-means is a hard-assignment, small-variance limit under equal mixing weights and spherical covariance.

text:
2 The objective
Given nn observations 𝒙1,…,𝒙n∈ℝp\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n\in\mathbb R^p, k-means seeks a partition C1,…,CkC_1,\dots,C_k and centers 𝝁1,…,𝝁k\boldsymbol\mu_1,\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k that minimize the within-cluster sum of squares,
W(C,𝝁)=∑j=1k∑i∈Cj‖𝒙i−𝝁j‖2.
W(C,\boldsymbol\mu)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2.

For a fixed partition the best center is the cluster mean, and WW then equals half the average squared distance between members of the same cluster:
∑i∈Cj‖𝒙i−𝒙‾j‖2=12|Cj|∑i∈Cj∑i′∈Cj‖𝒙i−𝒙i′‖2.
\sum_{i\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_j\rVert^2
=\frac{1}{2|C_j|}\sum_{i\in C_j}\sum_{i'\in C_j}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_{i'}\rVert^2.

So k-means is a statement about pairwise Euclidean distances within clusters. Finding the smallest possible WW can require comparing too many groupings to be practical. Common algorithms improve an initial grouping step by step, but can stop even when a different grouping would have a smaller WW. Trying several starting points and keeping the result with the smallest WW helps, although it does not guarantee the best possible grouping.

title: 6.2 k-Means and k-Medoids
text:
3 Lloyd’s algorithm
Lloyd’s algorithm alternates two steps from an initial set of centers.

Assignment. Give each observation to its nearest center: Cj={i:j=arg⁡min⁡l‖𝒙i−𝝁l‖}C_j=\{i:\ j=\arg\min_l\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_l\rVert\}.
Update. Replace each center by the mean of its members: 𝝁j=1|Cj|∑i∈Cj𝒙i\boldsymbol\mu_j=\frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{i\in C_j}\mathbf x_i.

Each step minimizes WW over one set of variables with the other held fixed, so WW never increases, and because there are finitely many partitions the algorithm terminates. Where it terminates depends on where it started.

3.2 k-means++ seeding
Random seeding often places two initial centers in the same dense region. k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) chooses the first center uniformly and each later center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest center already chosen,
P(choose 𝒙i)=D(𝒙i)2∑i′D(𝒙i′)2,
P(\text{choose }\mathbf x_i)=\frac{D(\mathbf x_i)^2}{\sum_{i'}D(\mathbf x_{i'})^2},

text:
4 Choosing k
Three common criteria answer slightly different questions.

4.1 The elbow
Plot WkW_k, the optimized objective for each kk. It always decreases; the “elbow” is where additional clusters stop buying much.

k_values <- 1:10
within <- sapply(k_values, function(k) kmeans(X, k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)$tot.withinss)



4.2 The silhouette
For observation ii in cluster AA, let aia_i be its mean distance to the other members of AA and bib_i the smallest mean distance to the members of any other cluster. The silhouette width is
si=bi−aimax⁡(ai,bi)∈[−1,1].
s_i=\frac{b_i-a_i}{\max(a_i,b_i)}\in[-1,1].

Values near 1 mean the observation sits well inside its cluster, near 0 that it lies between two clusters, and below 0 that it is probably in the wrong cluster. The average silhouette over all observations scores a clustering, and the kk with the largest average is a common choice.

D <- dist(X)
silhouette_means <- sapply(2:10, function(k) {
  fit <- kmeans(X, k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
  mean(silhouette(fit$cluster, D)[, "sil_width"])
})



4.3 The gap statistic
The gap statistic (Tibshirani, Walther, and Hastie, 2001) compares log⁡Wk\log W_k with its expected value under a reference distribution with no cluster structure, typically uniform over the range of each feature:
Gap⁡(k)=E*[logWk*]−log⁡Wk,
\operatorname{Gap}(k)=E^{*}\!\left[\log W_k^{*}\right]-\log W_k,

where the expectation is estimated from BB reference data sets. The recommended rule chooses the smallest kk such that Gap⁡(k)≥Gap⁡(k+1)−sk+1\operatorname{Gap}(k)\ge\operatorname{Gap}(k+1)-s_{k+1}, where sk+1s_{k+1} is the standard error of the reference simulations.

set.seed(431)
gap <- clusGap(X, FUN = function(x, k) kmeans(x, k, nstart = 10, iter.max = 100), K.max = 10, B = 50)
gap_table <- as.data.frame(gap$Tab)
gap_k <- maxSE(gap_table$gap, gap_table$SE.sim, method = "firstSEmax")


criteria <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(k = k_values, value = within, criterion = "within-cluster SS"),
  data.frame(k = 2:10, value = silhouette_means, criterion = "average silhouette"),
  data.frame(k = 1:10, value = gap_table$gap, criterion = "gap statistic")
)

ggplot(criteria, aes(k, value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#03a9e6") +
  geom_point(color = "#03a9e6") +
  facet_wrap(~criterion, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

text:
7 What k-means assumes

Clusters are spherical and similar in size in the standardized space, because every observation goes to the nearest center by Euclidean distance.
Every observation belongs to exactly one cluster, with no notion of uncertainty or of outliers.
kk is known. The algorithm has no internal reason to prefer one kk over another.
The scale of the features is meaningful, so standardization and weighting decide the result.

Each of the next three tutorials relaxes one of these: hierarchical clustering removes the fixed kk, mixture models add elongated clusters and soft membership, and density-based methods add outliers and arbitrary shapes.

title: Lecture 6: Clustering Methods for Sport
text:
What kinds of players are there, and which players are alike?
Positions are labels handed down by tradition. A modern NBA roster contains centers who shoot threes, forwards who run the offense, and guards who never handle the ball. Clustering asks the data instead of the label: given a set of measurements for each player, which players belong together, how many groups are there, and how confident should we be in the answer?
This lecture treats clustering as a modeling decision rather than a button to press. It builds up from the classical algorithms to the choices that actually determine the result:

Representation and distance. What to measure, how to transform and weight it, and what “far apart” means.
k-means and k-medoids. The workhorse algorithms, implemented from scratch and then with packages, with rules for choosing the number of clusters.
Hierarchical clustering. Trees of players, linkage rules, and the difference between archetypes and comparables.
Gaussian mixture models. Clustering as a probability model fitted by the EM algorithm, with soft memberships, model selection by BIC, and a Bayesian view.
Density-based, graph-based, and factorization methods. DBSCAN and HDBSCAN, spectral clustering, and non-negative matrix factorization for shot charts.
Validation. Internal indexes, bootstrap stability, agreement with external labels, and honest communication.

title: Lecture 6: Clustering Methods for Sport
text:
What kinds of players are there, and which players are alike?
Positions are labels handed down by tradition. A modern NBA roster contains centers who shoot threes, forwards who run the offense, and guards who never handle the ball. Clustering asks the data instead of the label: given a set of measurements for each player, which players belong together, how many groups are there, and how confident should we be in the answer?
This lecture treats clustering as a modeling decision rather than a button to press. It builds up from the classical algorithms to the choices that actually determine the result:

Representation and distance. What to measure, how to transform and weight it, and what “far apart” means.
k-means and k-medoids. The workhorse algorithms, implemented from scratch and then with packages, with rules for choosing the number of clusters.
Hierarchical clustering. Trees of players, linkage rules, and the difference between archetypes and comparables.
Gaussian mixture models. Clustering as a probability model fitted by the EM algorithm, with soft memberships, model selection by BIC, and a Bayesian view.
Density-based, graph-based, and factorization methods. DBSCAN and HDBSCAN, spectral clustering, and non-negative matrix factorization for shot charts.
Validation. Internal indexes, bootstrap stability, agreement with external labels, and honest communication.

text:
2 Learning without a target
Lectures 2 through 5 were supervised: every model had an outcome, and a held-out outcome told us whether the model was any good. Clustering has no outcome. We choose what “similar” means, an algorithm groups similar observations, and the only judge of the result is whether it is stable, interpretable, and useful for the question that motivated it.
That changes what a clustering can claim. “These players form five groups” is a statement about our distance, our features, and our algorithm as much as about the players. Three consequences follow.

The features and the distance are modeling decisions and should be designed for the question, not left at software defaults.
The number of clusters is not a fact to be discovered; it is a resolution to be chosen, and different resolutions answer different questions.
Validation means checking that the structure is real (not an artifact of the algorithm) and stable (not an artifact of the sample), which is the subject of Tutorial 6.6.

5 Five decisions in a dissimilarity
Akhanli and Hennig describe a dissimilarity as the result of five explicit steps. Each one changes the clustering.

5.1 1. Representation
Totals confound role with playing time: a starter and a backup with identical per-minute production have very different season totals. Per-36-minute rates remove playing time. Shares such as three-point attempts divided by all attempts remove volume as well, leaving shot selection. Which representation is right depends on the question: for archetypes of play style, rates and shares; for a player’s total contribution, totals.

5.2 2. Transformation
A difference of one block per 36 minutes means something different near zero than it does at three. Skewed variables let a few extreme players dominate distances.

bind_rows(
  data.frame(value = profiles$blk_36, scale = "blocks per 36"),
  data.frame(value = sqrt(profiles$blk_36), scale = "square root of blocks per 36")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#03a9e6", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Players") +
  theme_minimal()




Blocks per 36 minutes before and after a square-root transformation.




The transformation is a statement about which differences matter. Under the square root, the gap between 0 and 1 block counts more than the gap between 3 and 4, which is usually the intent.


5.3 3. Standardization
Points per 36 minutes ranges over about 30 units; effective field-goal percentage ranges over about 0.3. Without rescaling, the points variable alone would decide the distance. The usual fix is the z-score,
zik=xik−x‾ksk,
z_{ik}=\frac{x_{ik}-\bar x_k}{s_k},

which gives every variable unit variance. Alternatives are range scaling, (x−min⁡)/(max⁡−min⁡)(x-\min)/(\max-\min), and robust scaling by the median and median absolute deviation, which resists outliers.

X <- profile_matrix(profiles)
round(apply(X, 2, sd)[1:6], 3)

      1       1       1       1       1       1 




5.4 4. Weighting
Standardization makes every variable count equally, which is itself a choice. If the question is about offensive role, shot selection variables deserve more weight than steals. A weighted Euclidean distance is
dw(𝒙i,𝒙j)=∑k=1pwk(zik−zjk)2,
d_w(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\left(z_{ik}-z_{jk}\right)^2},

and multiplying column kk by wk\sqrt{w_k} before an unweighted algorithm has the same effect. Weights also handle redundancy: including points, field-goal attempts, and free-throw attempts triple-counts scoring volume unless their weights are reduced.


5.5 5. Aggregation
The Minkowski family combines per-variable differences,
dq(𝒙i,𝒙j)=(∑k=1pwk|zik−zjk|q)1/q,
d_q(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{p}w_k\left|z_{ik}-z_{jk}\right|^q\right)^{1/q},

with q=2q=2 (Euclidean) and q=1q=1 (Manhattan) the common cases. Euclidean distance emphasizes large differences on single variables; Manhattan distance treats a difference of 2 on one variable the same as differences of 1 on two variables.

title: 6.1 Unsupervised Learning: Goals, Features, and Distances
text:
6 Distances that measure different things

6.1 Correlation distance
Two players with the same pattern of strengths but different overall levels are close under the correlation distance
dcor(𝒙i,𝒙j)=1−r(𝒙i,𝒙j),
d_{\text{cor}}(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=1-r(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j),

where rr is the Pearson correlation between their standardized feature vectors. A high-usage scorer and a low-usage scorer with the same shape of profile are neighbors here and far apart under Euclidean distance.


6.2 Mahalanobis distance
Correlated features double-count. Points, field-goal attempts, and free-throw attempts move together, so Euclidean distance on all three is roughly three times the distance on one. The Mahalanobis distance
dM(𝒙i,𝒙j)=(𝒙i−𝒙j)𝖳S−1(𝒙i−𝒙j)
d_M(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=\sqrt{(\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j)^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}(\mathbf x_i-\mathbf x_j)}

divides by the covariance matrix SS, which removes the double-counting. It is Euclidean distance after decorrelating the features, and it is the natural distance inside a Gaussian mixture model (Tutorial 6.4).


6.3 Gower distance for mixed data
When some variables are categorical, such as handedness or position, Gower’s coefficient averages per-variable dissimilarities that are each scaled to [0,1][0,1]: absolute differences divided by the range for numeric variables and a 0/1 mismatch for categorical ones. cluster::daisy() computes it; Tutorial 6.5 uses it.

Two things stand out. Position groups occupy different regions but overlap heavily, so any clustering will disagree with the labels for many players. And there are no empty gaps between groups: the players form a continuum with denser and sparser regions, not islands. Clustering will impose boundaries on that continuum, which is why validation matters.

8.1 PCA as preprocessing
Clustering on the first few components has three effects: it removes noise in the small components, it decorrelates the features (so Euclidean distance on scores is Mahalanobis-like on the original variables when all components are kept), and it makes the result plottable. It also has a cost: PCA maximizes variance, not cluster separation, and a direction that separates two rare roles can be discarded as low-variance. Keeping enough components to explain about 80 to 90% of variance is a common compromise, and Tutorial 6.6 checks whether the clusters change.

9 Practice

Why do per-36 rates rather than totals suit a study of play style, and when would totals be preferable?
Two players have profiles (3,1,1)(3, 1, 1) and (1,3,1)(1, 3, 1) on three standardized variables. Compute their Euclidean, Manhattan, and correlation distances.
Explain why Mahalanobis distance can be preferable to Euclidean when several features measure scoring volume.
What is lost when clustering is done on the first two principal components only?







TipShow answers






Rates remove playing time, which is a role decision made by the coach rather than a characteristic of the player’s style; totals are preferable when the question concerns total contribution or availability.
Euclidean 4+4+0=2.83\sqrt{4+4+0}=2.83; Manhattan 2+2+0=42+2+0=4; the vectors have correlation −0.5-0.5 so the correlation distance is 1.51.5.
Correlated features count the same information several times in a Euclidean distance; the covariance inverse removes that redundancy so each independent dimension of variation counts once.
Directions of small variance that may nonetheless separate real groups, and any structure orthogonal to the two retained components.

title: 6.1 Unsupervised Learning: Goals, Features, and Distances
text:
10 Key takeaways

Clustering has no outcome to check against; the features and distance are modeling decisions that define the answer.
Decide first whether the goal is a few archetypes or many comparables.
Build a dissimilarity in five deliberate steps: representation, transformation, standardization, weighting, and aggregation.
Euclidean, Manhattan, correlation, Mahalanobis, and Gower distances answer different questions and produce different neighbors.
Principal components reveal that players form a continuum; clustering draws boundaries on it and must be validated.

text:
2 From points to a tree
k-means produces one partition at one resolution. Hierarchical clustering produces a tree that contains a partition at every resolution, from nn singletons to one cluster. The agglomerative version builds the tree bottom-up:

start with every observation in its own cluster;
merge the two closest clusters;
update the distances between the new cluster and every other cluster; and
repeat until one cluster remains.

The only decision is how to measure the distance between two clusters when we only have distances between points. That decision is the linkage rule, and different rules produce very different trees.

Ward’s criterion merges the pair whose union has the smallest increase in the k-means objective,
Δ(A,B)=∑i∈A∪B‖𝒙i−𝒙‾A∪B‖2−∑i∈A‖𝒙i−𝒙‾A‖2−∑i∈B‖𝒙i−𝒙‾B‖2=|A||B||A|+|B|‖𝒙‾A−𝒙‾B‖2.
\Delta(A,B)=\sum_{i\in A\cup B}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_{A\cup B}\rVert^2-\sum_{i\in A}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_A\rVert^2-\sum_{i\in B}\lVert\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_B\rVert^2
=\frac{|A||B|}{|A|+|B|}\lVert\bar{\mathbf x}_A-\bar{\mathbf x}_B\rVert^2.

The last form shows that Ward is a centroid distance weighted by cluster sizes, which discourages absorbing a large cluster into a small one.

4 Build the trees

linkages <- c("single", "complete", "average", "ward.D2")
trees <- lapply(linkages, function(method) hclust(D, method = method))
names(trees) <- linkages

ward.D2 applies Ward’s criterion to the Euclidean distances as intended; the older ward.D option expects squared distances.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 4, 2, 1))
for (method in linkages) {
  plot(trees[[method]], labels = FALSE, main = method, xlab = "", sub = "", hang = -1)
}




Dendrograms of the 360 player profiles under four linkage rules.




Single linkage chains one player at a time onto a growing blob, which is its usual behavior on data without gaps. Complete and Ward linkage produce balanced branches. Average linkage sits between them.

4.1 Reading a dendrogram

The height at which two branches join is the linkage distance at that merge. Two players joined near the bottom are close; two branches joined near the top are far apart.
The left-right order is arbitrary. Any branch can be flipped without changing the tree, so adjacency along the bottom means nothing unless the two leaves share a low merge.
A long vertical gap below a merge means the merged groups were well separated at that resolution; cutting the tree inside a long gap gives a stable partition.



4.2 The cophenetic correlation
The tree implies a distance between every pair of players: the height at which they are first joined, called the cophenetic distance. The correlation between the cophenetic distances and the original distances measures how faithfully the tree represents the data.

data.frame(
  linkage = linkages,
  cophenetic_correlation = sapply(trees, function(tree) cor(D, cophenetic(tree)))
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

Ward’s method follows a different objective: limiting increases in within-cluster squared variation.

)
example_distances <- dist(cophenetic_example)
example_tree <- hclust(example_distances, method = "average")
example_cophenetic <- cophenetic(example_tree)

data.frame(

) %>% knitr::kable(digits = 3)

What this checks: how faithfully the tree summarizes the chosen distances. It does not choose a number of clusters or prove that useful player groups exist. See the R documentation for cophenetic distances.

A partition is obtained by cutting the tree at a height or by asking for kk clusters.

ward <- trees[["ward.D2"]]
cuts <- sapply(c(2, 4, 6, 8, 12), function(k) cutree(ward, k = k))
colnames(cuts) <- paste0("k_", c(2, 4, 6, 8, 12))

apply(cuts, 2, function(labels) paste(sort(table(labels), decreasing = TRUE), collapse = ", ")) %>%
  data.frame(cluster_sizes = .) %>%

  adjusted_rand_index = adjusted_rand_index(profiles$ward_6, kmeans_6$cluster),

Ward and k-means optimize the same objective, but Ward is greedy and never revisits a merge, so its within-cluster sum of squares is noticeably larger and the two partitions differ at many boundaries. A common practice is to use Ward’s solution as the starting point for k-means, which keeps the interpretability of the tree and polishes the partition.

6 Comparables from the tree
Cutting the tree low produces many small clusters, the “comparables” use of Tutorial 6.1. At k=40k=40 the average cluster holds about nine players.

profiles$ward_40 <- cutree(ward, k = 40)

comparables <- function(name) {
  cluster <- profiles$ward_40[profiles$player == name]
  profiles %>%
    filter(ward_40 == cluster, player != name) %>%
    arrange(desc(minutes)) %>%
    pull(player)
}

data.frame(
  player = c("Jalen Brunson", "Rudy Gobert", "Mikal Bridges"),
  comparables = sapply(c("Jalen Brunson", "Rudy Gobert", "Mikal Bridges"), function(p) paste(head(comparables(p), 6), collapse = ", "))
) %>%

title: 6.3 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
7 Divisive clustering
The top-down alternative, DIANA (divisive analysis), starts with one cluster and repeatedly splits the cluster with the largest diameter by moving out the observation with the largest average dissimilarity and then everyone closer to the splinter group. It is more expensive but makes its biggest decisions first, which can matter when the top-level structure is what you want.

diana_fit <- diana(D)
data.frame(
  comparison = "DIANA (k = 6) versus Ward (k = 6)",
  adjusted_rand_index = adjusted_rand_index(cutree(as.hclust(diana_fit), k = 6), profiles$ward_6),
  divisive_coefficient = diana_fit$dc
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)









comparison
adjusted_rand_index
divisive_coefficient




DIANA (k = 6) versus Ward (k = 6)
0.346
0.842





The divisive coefficient, like the agglomerative coefficient of agnes(), measures the strength of the clustering structure found (values near 1 mean clear structure). Values in the middle of the range are typical for player data.

title: 6.3 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
8 Strengths and weaknesses
Hierarchical clustering offers:

a result at every resolution from one run, with nested partitions;
freedom to use any dissimilarity, including Gower and correlation distances; and
a picture, the dendrogram, that communicates structure without choosing kk first.

Its costs are:

O(n2)O(n^2) memory, which rules out very large data sets;
greedy merges that are never revised, so a bad early merge persists; and
strong dependence on the linkage rule, which must be justified rather than defaulted.

text:
9 Practice

Three clusters have pairwise distances d(A,B)=2d(A,B)=2, d(A,C)=5d(A,C)=5, d(B,C)=4d(B,C)=4. After merging AA and BB, what is the distance to CC under single, complete, and average linkage if |A|=|B||A|=|B|?
Why can centroid linkage produce a merge at a lower height than an earlier merge, and why can Ward and average linkage not?
Explain why cutting a tree at k=6k=6 and at k=7k=7 gives partitions that agree on all but one cluster.
A dendrogram shows two players adjacent at the bottom. What, if anything, does that imply about their distance?







TipShow answers






Single min⁡(5,4)=4\min(5,4)=4; complete max⁡(5,4)=5\max(5,4)=5; average (5+4)/2=4.5(5+4)/2=4.5.
The centroid of a merged cluster can be closer to a third cluster than either original centroid was, violating monotonicity; single, complete, average, and Ward distances never decrease after a merge.
The tree is nested: the seven-cluster partition is obtained from the six-cluster partition by splitting exactly one cluster.
Nothing by itself. Adjacent leaves may belong to branches that join near the top; only the merge height carries information.

title: 6.3 Hierarchical Clustering
text:
10 Key takeaways

Agglomerative clustering builds a nested tree; the linkage rule defines the distance between clusters and shapes everything.
Single linkage chains, complete and Ward compact, average compromises; the Lance-Williams recursion runs them all.
Read heights, not horizontal order; use the cophenetic correlation to judge the tree’s fidelity.
Cut high for archetypes and low for comparables; the same tree serves both.

title: 6.5 Beyond the Classics: Density, Graphs, and Matrix Factorization
text:
2 What the classics cannot do

2.1 Compactness versus connectedness
Before choosing a clustering method, decide what it should mean for points to belong together.

Compactness: members sit close to a common center. Think of players whose standardized statistics all resemble one typical profile.
Connectedness: members can reach one another through a chain of short steps between nearby observations. The ends of the chain can be far apart, so a curved group may have no useful central representative.







Figure 1: Compact groups gather around centers, while connected groups can follow curved chains of nearby points.



In the left panel, a center summarizes each group well. In the right panel, following neighbors preserves each crescent even though its endpoints are far apart. These are two useful notions of a cluster, rather than guarantees about what any algorithm will recover. The distance and neighborhood settings determine which points count as neighbors.
k-means favors compact groups around centroids. Ward linkage favors merges with small increases in squared error. Gaussian components can be elongated, but each component remains an elliptical density and an ordinary mixture assigns all observations membership probabilities. Density and graph methods offer additional ways to represent connected regions and unusual observations.

text:
3 Density-based clustering
Density-based methods combine connectedness with a crowding requirement: a cluster needs a chain of sufficiently dense neighborhoods. For shot locations, imagine sliding a small circle around the court and asking whether enough shots fall inside it.

3.1 DBSCAN
DBSCAN (Ester et al., 1996) defines clusters as connected regions of high density. With a radius ε\varepsilon and a minimum count mm:

a core point has at least mm points (including itself) within distance ε\varepsilon;
a border point is within ε\varepsilon of a core point but is not itself a core point;
a noise point is neither.

Two core points within ε\varepsilon of each other are connected, and a cluster is a maximal set of connected core points together with their border points. Noise points belong to no cluster. The algorithm has no kk; the number of clusters is whatever the density produces.


3.2 How DBSCAN grows a cluster
Suppose we use eps = 2.2 feet and minPts = 5 on shot locations. A shot with four other shots within 2.2 feet is a core point because it counts itself as the fifth. A nearby shot with only two other neighbors is a border point if its circle reaches a core point. An isolated shot that reaches no core point is noise.

Start at an unvisited core point and give it a new cluster label.
Add its neighbors. Whenever a newly reached neighbor is also core, explore that point’s neighborhood too.
Stop when no more core neighborhoods can extend the cluster, then start again at another unvisited core point.

Only core points extend a cluster. A chain consisting only of border points cannot bridge two dense groups. A border point touching two clusters can receive an order-dependent assignment. The final noise points remain unassigned, which R records as cluster 0.


3.3 Choosing the parameters
The two settings answer different questions:








Setting
Meaning
What changing it tends to do




eps (ε\varepsilon)
How far does a neighborhood reach?
A larger radius connects more points and can merge groups; a smaller radius can split groups and leave more noise.


minPts (mm)
How many points make a neighborhood dense?
A larger count makes core status harder to earn and can leave more noise.



Distances use the supplied feature units. Standardize player statistics before computing distances; court coordinates already share a unit, feet. An epsilon suitable for shot coordinates has no direct meaning for principal-component scores.
Because dbscan::dbscan() counts the point itself in minPts = m, plot distances to the (m−1)(m-1)-th other nearest neighbor. Start with a dimension-aware value of minPts, then examine sensitivity to both parameters. Points inside dense regions have small values; the curve bends upward where noise begins, and the bend is a natural ε\varepsilon.

pcs <- prcomp(X, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)$x[, 1:5]
knn_distances <- sort(kNNdist(pcs, k = 4))

ggplot(data.frame(rank = seq_along(knn_distances), distance = knn_distances), aes(rank, distance)) +
  geom_line(color = "#03a9e6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.6, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  labs(x = "Players, sorted", y = "Distance to 4th nearest neighbor") +
  theme_minimal()




Sorted distance to the fourth-nearest neighbor for every player profile. The knee marks a candidate epsilon.




The dashed line at 1.6 is the candidate used below, not an automatically estimated cutoff. A knee can be ambiguous or absent. Try nearby radii and counts, then compare the number of clusters, the fraction labeled noise, and whether the groups remain interpretable. Here five PCs with minPts = 5 illustrate the mechanics; higher-dimensional data often need a larger count, so this setting is not a default recommendation.

3.5 Shot locations for one player
Density has a more natural role for shot locations, where the clusters are spatial regions.

player_shots <- shots %>% filter(shooter == "Stephen Curry", court_y >= -2)
S <- as.matrix(player_shots[, c("court_x", "court_y")])
nrow(S)

[1] 1460

table(cluster = db_shots$cluster)

cluster

215 778 358  25  26  45  13

  ggplot(aes(court_x, court_y, color = cluster)) +

DBSCAN on one player’s shot locations. Gray points are noise; colored points are density clusters.




DBSCAN finds the regions where this player shoots often and labels the rest as scattered attempts, without any assumption that the regions are round. Its weakness is visible too: one ε\varepsilon must serve every region, so a dense rim cluster and a diffuse arc cluster cannot both be resolved well.


3.6 HDBSCAN
HDBSCAN (Campello, Moulavi, and Sander, 2013) explores many density thresholds instead of choosing one global ε\varepsilon. Imagine gradually shrinking DBSCAN’s neighborhood radius: broad regions break into smaller, denser groups. HDBSCAN tracks which groups survive across density levels.
Its main steps are:

Estimate a core distance for each point: how far it must reach to collect enough neighbors. A sparse area needs a larger distance.
Compare points using mutual reachability distance, the largest of their ordinary distance and their two core distances. This makes a connection through a sparse area more costly.
Build a minimum spanning tree, a set of links that connects all points with the smallest total link weight and no loops. Removing links from largest to smallest creates a hierarchy of groups.
Select groups with high stability, which combines their membership and persistence across density levels, rather than taking one horizontal cut through the whole hierarchy.

This allows dense and more diffuse clusters to coexist, although overlapping groups or weak density separation can still be difficult. In dbscan::hdbscan(), minPts controls smoothing and minimum cluster size. With its self-counting convention, the core distance uses the (m−1)(m-1)-th other nearest neighbor. Other implementations can expose smoothing and minimum size as separate settings.

hdb <- hdbscan(S, minPts = 15)
table(cluster = hdb$cluster)

cluster
  0   1   2   3   4   5   6 
180  19  41  24 765  26 405 



player_shots %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(hdb$cluster)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(court_x, court_y, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "gray70", scales::hue_pal()(max(hdb$cluster)))) +
  court_layers() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal()




HDBSCAN on the same shots, with clusters selected by stability across density levels.




The R implementation returns membership_prob, a density-based membership strength. Despite its name, this score is not a Bayesian posterior probability or a Gaussian-mixture responsibility, and it does not sum over alternative clusters in the same way.

title: 6.5 Beyond the Classics: Density, Graphs, and Matrix Factorization
text:
4 Spectral clustering
Spectral clustering represents the data as a graph: each observation is a node, and a link joins observations that are neighbors. A strong link means high similarity. The goal is to divide this network into groups with strong connections inside each group and relatively weak connections between groups.
Think of shots arranged along two separate curved bands. Shots at opposite ends of one band may be far apart, but a chain of nearby shots connects them. A graph can preserve that chain, whereas k-means in the original coordinates favors points near the same center. Spectral clustering still uses distances to build its graph; it changes how those local distances become a grouping.
Unlike DBSCAN, the version here requires a chosen number of clusters kk and assigns every observation to a group. It has no automatic noise label.

4.1 Reading the graph matrices







Object
Plain-language role




WW
Similarity table: WijW_{ij} is the strength of the link from point ii to point jj; zero means no link. We set Wii=0W_{ii}=0.


DD
Diagonal table of total connection strength: Dii=∑jWijD_{ii}=\sum_j W_{ij}. A well-connected point has a larger degree.


L=D−WL=D-W
Graph Laplacian: summarizes how a value at each point differs from the values at its neighbors.


LsymL_{\text{sym}}
Normalized Laplacian: adjusts for differences in total connection strength between points.





4.2 Similarity graph and Laplacian
Build a weighted graph with vertices at the observations and edges between neighbors,
Wij=exp⁡(−d(𝒙i,𝒙j)2σiσj)if i is a neighbor of j or vice versa, else 0,
W_{ij}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)^2}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}\right)
\quad\text{if } i \text{ is a neighbor of } j \text{ or vice versa, else } 0,

with local scales σi\sigma_i equal to the distance to the qq-th other nearest neighbor. Here qq is the graph neighborhood size (the helper’s neighbors argument), separate from DBSCAN’s minPts. Close pairs receive larger weights; distant pairs receive smaller weights. Let DD be the diagonal matrix of degrees di=∑jWijd_i=\sum_j W_{ij}. The graph Laplacian and its symmetric normalization are
L=D−W,Lsym=I−D−1/2WD−1/2.
L=D-W,
\qquad
L_{\text{sym}}=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}.

For any vector 𝒇\mathbf f,
𝒇𝖳L𝒇=12∑i,jWij(fi−fj)2,
\mathbf f^{\mathsf T}L\mathbf f=\frac12\sum_{i,j}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2,

where fif_i is a number attached to node ii. If two strongly linked nodes get very different values, the squared difference produces a large penalty. For example, a link of weight 1 with values 0 and 1 contributes 1 to the energy after the two symmetric terms combine; a link of weight 0.1 contributes only 0.1. It is therefore cheaper to put a boundary across weak links.
An eigenvector supplies one value per node, so we can use it as a new coordinate for each observation. Eigenvectors with small eigenvalues capture gradual variation across strongly linked parts of the graph. For the normalized Laplacian, this smoothness applies to values adjusted by the square root of degree. Using several such coordinates gives a graph embedding, a new representation in which groups linked by chains can become easier to separate.
Mathematically, this approximates a normalized cut: it seeks weak links between groups while accounting for each group’s total connection strength, so that isolating a tiny group is less attractive than under an unnormalized cut. With positive degrees, the number of eigenvalues exactly zero equals the number of disconnected components. Several small eigenvalues followed by a large eigengap can suggest a cluster count, but near-zero values alone do not prove there are separate components.


4.3 The algorithm

Choose kk and a neighborhood size, then form WW, DD, and LsymL_{\text{sym}}. Check for isolated nodes before dividing by degrees.
Take the kk eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues as the columns of U∈ℝn×kU\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}. Each row now describes one observation using kk graph coordinates.
Normalize each nonzero row to length one, so clustering compares the direction of these graph coordinates.
Run k-means on the rows of UU to obtain the final kk labels.

For 400 observations and k=2k=2, WW is a 400×400400\times400 table, while UU has 400 rows and just two columns. The last step clusters these two new coordinates. It does not rerun k-means on the original x,yx,y coordinates.
The graph is a modeling choice. Too few neighbors can fragment one group; too many can connect two groups that should stay separate. Standardization, the similarity scale, and kk also affect the result. Compare nearby settings rather than treating the graph as fixed truth.


4.4 Why k-means can split curved groups

  moons$x <- moons$x + rnorm(2 * n, 0, noise)
  moons$y <- moons$y + rnorm(2 * n, 0, noise)
  moons
}

5 Mixed data: Gower distance and k-medoids
Real scouting data mix numbers with categories: position, handedness, contract type, college conference. Gower’s coefficient handles them by averaging per-variable dissimilarities, each scaled to [0,1][0,1]:
dG(i,j)=∑kwkδijkdijk∑kwkδijk,dijk={|xik−xjk|rangeknumeric,𝟙{xik≠xjk}categorical,
d_G(i,j)=\frac{\sum_k w_k\,\delta_{ijk}\,d_{ijk}}{\sum_k w_k\,\delta_{ijk}},
\qquad
d_{ijk}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{|x_{ik}-x_{jk}|}{\text{range}_k} & \text{numeric},\\[8pt]
\mathbb 1\{x_{ik}\ne x_{jk}\} & \text{categorical},

6 Non-negative matrix factorization for shot charts
A player’s shot chart is a vector of counts over court cells. Stack the charts of nn players into a matrix V∈ℝ≥0n×mV\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}_{\ge0} with one row per player and one column per cell. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) seeks
V≈WH,W∈ℝ≥0n×r,H∈ℝ≥0r×m,
V\approx WH,
\qquad
W\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}_{\ge0},
\quad
H\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}_{\ge0},

by minimizing ‖V−WH‖F2\lVert V-WH\rVert_F^2. The rows of HH are rr basis charts, each a non-negative pattern over the court, and row ii of WW says how much of each basis player ii uses. Because nothing can be negative, the bases are additive parts, which for shot charts turn out to be shot types: rim, corner threes, above-the-break threes, and so on. This is the approach of Miller, Bornn, Adams, and Goldsberry (2014), who used it to define shooting styles.
NMF differs from PCA in two ways. Its components are non-negative and therefore interpretable as charts, whereas principal components have negative entries. And it is a soft description: a player is a mixture of bases, not a member of a cluster.

6.1 Multiplicative updates
Lee and Seung (2001) showed that the updates
H←H⊙W𝖳VW𝖳WH,W←W⊙VH𝖳WHH𝖳,
H\leftarrow H\odot\frac{W^{\mathsf T}V}{W^{\mathsf T}WH},
\qquad
W\leftarrow W\odot\frac{VH^{\mathsf T}}{WHH^{\mathsf T}},

with ⊙\odot and the fraction taken elementwise, never increase the loss and keep every entry non-negative. They are a form of gradient descent with a step size chosen to preserve the sign.

8 Practice

With ε\varepsilon fixed, what happens to the number of noise points as mm increases?
Why does spectral clustering succeed on the half-moons where k-means fails?
Explain in one sentence why a k-means on NMF loadings and a k-means on raw shot charts can give different clusters.
Give one reason to prefer NMF over a Gaussian mixture for shot charts.







TipShow answers






It increases: more points fail to have mm neighbors within ε\varepsilon, so fewer points are core points and more are left unassigned.
The moons are connected through chains of nearby points but are not compact around a center, so the graph embedding separates them while Euclidean distance to a centroid does not.
The loadings represent each chart in a low-dimensional space of shot types, which changes the representation and can reduce cell-level noise, whereas raw charts are dominated by the high-count rim cells.
NMF returns interpretable non-negative basis charts and describes each player as a mixture, whereas a mixture over shot coordinates describes zones for individual shots rather than styles for players.

text:
9 Key takeaways

DBSCAN and HDBSCAN find clusters of arbitrary shape and label outliers; on player profiles, noise labels depend on the chosen features and density thresholds.
Spectral clustering partitions a similarity graph through the eigenvectors of its Laplacian and finds connected rather than compact clusters.
Gower distance makes mixed data clusterable with k-medoids or hierarchical methods; weights matter.
NMF decomposes shot charts into additive basis charts and per-player loadings, a soft and interpretable description of style.
